title: Menopause is an information and care-navigation gap with consequences for work and community participation
source_unit: Gallup-Pivotal Women's Health Survey, menopause and perimenopause findings
geography: United States; women and men surveyed online July 14-22, 2026

observations.period: July 14-22, 2026; knowledge and information sources around menopause

denominator.unit: U.S. women surveyed by Gallup-Pivotal; overall study also surveyed 1,296 men

symptom_understanding.unit: percent of women saying they have a good understanding of menopause symptoms

treatment_understanding.unit: percent saying they have a good understanding of treatment options

firsthand_learning.unit: percent of women who experienced menopause saying they learned about it only when they had symptoms

distributed_authority.value: Menopause knowledge is often acquired through lived experience and personal networks before formal clinical discussion, creating an information and navigation gap at a predictable life stage.

observations.method: Gallup-Pivotal Women's Health Survey conducted online July 14-22, 2026 among 3,845 women and 1,296 men via the Gallup Panel; public article reports self-assessed knowledge and information-source estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The public release does not provide all subgroup denominators, the full questionnaire, objective knowledge testing, information quality, treatment access, clinical outcomes or causal effects of information source.
observations.subgroup: U.S. women across age groups, including women who have and have not experienced menopause or perimenopause.
observations.counterinterpretation: Personal networks may provide useful experiential knowledge and complement clinicians; low reported understanding may reflect the complexity of treatment choices rather than absence of information.

denominator.unit: U.S. women surveyed by Gallup-Pivotal; source-use subgroup denominators vary

family_source.unit: percent who have encountered menopause information from family members

friend_source.unit: percent who have encountered information from friends

social_media_source.unit: percent who have encountered information on social media

medical_source.unit: percent who have encountered information from doctors or other medical professionals

ai_source.unit: percent who have used AI tools such as ChatGPT or chatbots for menopause information

provider_conversation.unit: percent of women who have ever discussed menopause with a healthcare provider

observations.method: Descriptive source-use and provider-conversation estimates from the Gallup-Pivotal survey.
observations.uncertainty: Source exposure is not source trust, accuracy, comprehension or care completion; multiple responses can overlap and the release does not establish why provider conversations are absent.
observations.subgroup: U.S. women; provider discussion rises substantially with age, from 5% among women age 18-34 to 63% among women age 45-54 and 73% among women age 55-64.
observations.counterinterpretation: Family, friends and social media may widen early awareness, while clinical conversations may occur later when symptoms become salient; the pattern does not prove that informal information displaces professional care.

observations.period: July 14-22, 2026; menopause-related care navigation and work/community effects

denominator.unit: U.S. women surveyed by Gallup-Pivotal; treatment and experienced-menopause subgroups vary

push_to_be_taken_seriously.unit: percent of women seeking or receiving treatment who had to push to be taken seriously or to receive treatment

multiple_providers.unit: percent who had to see multiple providers before symptoms were addressed or diagnosed

unable_to_get_care.unit: percent unable to get the care they felt they needed despite trying

work_life_effect.value: Among women who experienced menopause, 28% reported being limited in work effort, 22% stepped back from community involvement, 15% did not pursue a promotion, 12% reduced hours and 10% changed jobs.

care_to_participation_route.value: Recognition and continuity of care can determine whether a life-stage health transition remains manageable or becomes a work, self-care and civic-participation constraint.

observations.method: Descriptive treatment-experience and self-reported life-impact estimates from the Gallup-Pivotal Women's Health Survey.
observations.uncertainty: The associations are retrospective and self-reported; the study does not establish clinical severity, treatment effectiveness, employer accommodation, income loss, promotion causation or the counterfactual without menopause symptoms.
observations.subgroup: Women who have experienced menopause or perimenopause, and women age 35 and older seeking or receiving treatment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Work and community effects may reflect symptoms, caregiving, workplace conditions, discrimination, family obligations or other midlife transitions; care difficulty may be one contributing pathway among several.

related_sources.claim: Official Gallup article reports study sample, field dates, menopause knowledge, information sources, provider discussion, treatment barriers and work/community impacts.

boundary: This record adds a life-stage health-information and care-navigation route from distributed knowledge and provider access through recognition, treatment continuity, work, self-care and community participation. It does not measure objective knowledge, clinical severity, treatment effectiveness, employer response, causal career effects or universal menopause experience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Gallup article was reviewed for the Gallup-Pivotal sample and field dates, symptom and treatment understanding, source mix, provider discussion, treatment barriers, work/community impacts and priority framing.
